newsitem.title: CHINA: China tells U.S. not to let Taiwan visit harm ties.
newsitem.headline: China tells U.S. not to let Taiwan visit harm ties.

text.p: China on Thursday urged Washington to protect Sino-U.S. ties by blocking rival Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui from carrying out pro-independence activities during a transit visit to the United States.

A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman stopped short of demanding Washington refuse to issue Lee a transit visa but made clear that Beijing would be watching carefully to see how the planned Hawaii stopover was managed.

"We hope that the U.S. side will... not allow the eminent politicians of Taiwan to engage in the activities aimed at splitting the motherland... so as not to bring damage to Sino-U.S. relations," the spokesman said in a statement.

"The issue of Taiwan is always the most important and sensitive issue in the Sino-U.S. relations, and the proper handling of this issue is crucial to the development of a sound and stable Sino-U.S. relationship," he said.

The U.S. State Department said on Wednesday it expected to issue Lee a visa to allow him to transit through Honolulu on September 4-5 and September 17-18 on his way to and from an international conference in Panama.

The spokesman said Taiwan wanted to use such stopovers as opportunities to promote independence for the island, which has been communist Beijing's arch rival since defeated Nationalist forces fled there at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.

"It has been proven by bulk of facts that the real purpose of the Taiwanese eminent politicians' transit through America is to create "Two Chinas" or "One China, One Taiwan"... and at the same time attempt to damage the relations between China and the U.S.," the Chinese spokesman said.

Beijing, which regards Taiwan as a rebel province and seeks to isolate the island's authorities from the international arena, regularly accuse Lee and other Taiwan leaders of working toward a declaration of formal independence.
Taipei rejects the charge, saying it wants eventual reunification with the mainland but that Beijing must first match the island's introduction of democratic politics.

The U.S. State Department said in April Lee was eligible for a transit visa for use on his way to the meeting of Panama Canal users in the Central American nation, which is one of just 30 states that diplomatically recognise Taipei and not Beijing.

State Department spokesman James Foley said Washington expected Lee to respect the conditions under which such visas are issued -- a coded way of saying that the Taiwanese leader would be expected to refrain from political activities.
Sino-U.S. relations have only recently begun to recover from the diplomatic fall-out of a ground-breaking unofficial visit by Lee to the United States in June 1995.
That visit infuriated Beijing, which froze semi-official talks aimed at boosting cooperation with Taipei and launched months of menacing war games near the island.

While disputes over Taiwan, trade and human rights continue to dog ties, Washington and Beijing hope to put the seal on their recent rapprochement in October with a state visit to the United States by Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
